title: Gomarus and Piscator: only the sin against the Spirit is mortal as irremissible
source_text: XXVII. Praeterea nonnulli Doctores Reformati venialia quandoque appellant peccata omnia quae possunt, mediante poenitentia, remissionem & veniam consequi: mortale vero illud quod remitti non potest, sed mortem aeternam necessario affert. Quo sensu mortale est solum peccatum in Spiritum Sanctum, reliqua vero omnia peccata venialia. Adeo ut haec distinctio, eadem sit cum illa Joannis, capite quinto primae epistolae, ubi distinguit peccatum ad mortem, & peccatum quod non est ad mortem: & cum ea qua Scholae vulgo distinguunt peccatum in remissibile & irremissibile. Hoc sensu peccatum distinguunt in mortale & veniale Gomarus in Syntagmate Disputationum Leydensium, disp. 13. thes. 10. & Piscator, volumine primo Thesium Theologicarum, loco 7. disp. 3. th. 64.
pass_a_gloss: Besides, some Reformed doctors sometimes call venial all sins which can, through repentance, obtain remission and pardon: but mortal that which cannot be remitted, but necessarily brings eternal death. In which sense mortal is only the sin against the Holy Spirit, but all the remaining sins venial. So that this distinction is the same as that of John in the fifth chapter of the first epistle, where he distinguishes a sin unto death and a sin that is not unto death: and with that by which the Schools commonly distinguish sin into remissible and irremissible. In this sense Gomarus in the Syntagma of the Leyden Disputations, disputation 13, thesis 10, and Piscator in the first volume of Theological Theses, locus 7, disputation 3, thesis 64, distinguish sin into mortal and venial.
pass_b_english: Some Reformed reserve ‘mortal’ for the irremissible sin against the Spirit—all else ‘venial’ as remissible.
That matches 1 John’s sin unto death and Gomarus/Piscator’s usage.
